CausalChain: Dysregulated cell cycle in NSCLC (via aberrant p53/Rb) -> Impaired coordination of exosome biogenesis and ESCRT-mediated miRNA sorting -> Reduced exosomal miR-200 levels -> Sustained EMT/CSC states -> Increased chemoresistance -> (Intervention: inducible CRISPR/Cas9 modulation of p53/Rb & RNAi targeting ESCRT components) -> Restoration of ESCRT function & exosomal miR-200 enrichment -> Induction of MET & suppression of CSC traits -> Enhanced chemosensitivity
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that a synergistic intervention targeting both upstream cell cycle checkpoints and downstream exosome-sorting mechanisms will restore proper exosomal miR-200 packaging in NSCLC cells. Specifically, we propose that utilizing an inducible CRISPR/Cas9 system to finely modulate p53 and Rb levels, in combination with RNA interference (RNAi) to optimize ESCRT complex activity, will correct the aberrant exosome biogenesis associated with cell cycle dysregulation. This dual targeting will augment exosomal levels of miR-200, thereby promoting a phenotypic switch from EMT/CSC-like states to MET, and consequently, restoring chemosensitivity to tumor cells. Advanced technologies, including single-cell sequencing, digital droplet PCR, and live-cell imaging, will be employed to precisely delineate and validate each step of this mechanistic pathway.
Abstract: In non‐small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), dysregulation of cell cycle checkpoints—particularly via aberrations in key regulators such as p53 and Rb—has been implicated in altered exosome biogenesis and mis-sorting of microRNAs (miRNAs) including miR-200. We propose a refined, dual-modality intervention hypothesis that integrates precise, inducible modulation of the cell cycle with targeted regulation of exosomal sorting machinery (notably the ESCRT complexes) to restore miR-200 packaging. By employing tamoxifen-inducible CRISPR/Cas9 systems to fine-tune p53/Rb activity alongside RNA interference techniques aimed at modulating key ESCRT components, this strategy aims to re-establish appropriate exosomal miR-200 enrichment. In turn, this restoration is hypothesized to trigger a phenotypic shift from the epithelial-to-mesenchymal (EMT) and cancer stem cell (CSC)-like states toward a mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition (MET), enhancing chemosensitivity. The planned application of advanced methodologies such as single-cell sequencing, digital droplet PCR, and high-resolution live-cell imaging will ensure rigorous mapping and validation of each mechanistic link in this pathway.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis focused exclusively on modulating cell cycle checkpoints (via CRISPR/Cas9 targeting of p53/Rb) to indirectly correct exosomal miR-200 packaging. In the new hypothesis, we have refined this concept by incorporating a dual-modality approach that not only adjusts cell cycle dysregulation but also directly targets the exosome sorting machinery (e.g., via RNAi targeting of ESCRT components). This approach aims to address critiques that the original mechanism might be too indirect, given that miRNA dysregulation and exosomal sorting defects are also influenced by established genetic and epigenetic factors. The new hypothesis explicitly references each step of the original causal chain, reinforcing the links from cell cycle regulation through exosome biogenesis to miR-200-mediated phenotypic shifts and chemosensitivity, while leveraging contemporary inducible and high-precision technologies to enhance practical implementability.
